name: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate
lead: Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a lipophilic derivative of tranexamic acid, formulated as a cosmetic ingredient for topical skin-lightening and hyperpigmentation products. It is the cetyl ester of tranexamic acid supplied as a mesylate salt.[1][3]

Tranexamic acid itself is a hydrophilic zwitterionic molecule that is described as penetrating the stratum corneum poorly; formulators have used penetration enhancers, microneedling or lipophilic derivatives such as cetyl tranexamate mesylate to address this.[3] The derivative is marketed for uneven skin tone and post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation.

Published evidence is limited. A 2021 study in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology examined its safety and skin-lightening performance on sun-damaged skin,[1] and a small registered trial examined its effect on acne-related hyperpigmentation.[2]

paras: It is used in leave-on serums and creams aimed at dark spots, melasma-like discoloration and post-acne marks. The rationale is that attaching a cetyl (long fatty) chain makes the molecule more lipophilic than tranexamic acid, which may improve delivery through the skin barrier.[3]

Tranexamic acid is an antifibrinolytic; its proposed skin-lightening action involves reducing plasmin-related signalling that stimulates melanocytes. The cetyl ester is presented as a topical delivery form of this approach. Detailed pharmacokinetic data for the derivative are not available in the sources reviewed.

A 2021 report in the Journal of Cosmetic Dermatology investigated the safety and skin-lightening performance of cetyl tranexamate mesylate in sun-damaged skin, framing it as a new topical bioactive for hyperpigmentation and inflammation.[1] A separate registered study (NCT06080035), completed with 22 participants and started in November 2023, examined effects on the appearance of acne-related post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation; it is listed as a non-randomised (NA phase) study.[2] Larger independent randomised trials have not been identified. For the parent compound, a general reference notes that efficacy for melasma remained unproven as of 2017, with no large randomised trials.[3]

card.summary: A fat-soluble tranexamic acid ester put in serums for dark spots; early cosmetic-grade data, little independent testing.
card.note: Evidence is mostly small, manufacturer-linked studies.

quick.overview:
Cetyl tranexamate mesylate is a modified form of tranexamic acid designed for skincare. It appears in products aimed at hyperpigmentation, dark spots and post-acne marks.

Published human data are limited to a 2021 cosmetic-dermatology study and a small registered acne-hyperpigmentation trial; no large independent randomised trials were found.
quick.mechanism: Tranexamic acid is thought to reduce signalling that drives melanocyte pigment production. The cetyl chain makes the molecule more fat-soluble, intended to help it cross the skin barrier better than the parent compound.
quick.risks: Sources reviewed report no specific safety concerns, but long-term data are lacking. It is sold as a cosmetic ingredient; as with any topical, irritation is possible.
